note: English rendering of தம்மபதம்: முப்பத்தோர் நாள். The Tamil is the authoritative text; this translation is for readers who do not read Tamil and should be reviewed by the sangha before it is treated as official.
intro: First, my heartfelt thanks to the sangha for choosing me to take responsibility for this month. It is a great privilege, and at the same time a duty. I will try in full to be worthy of your trust.

This month I want to begin something new. From the first day of July to the last, one story each day. Stories from the Buddha's life; stories of the disciples closest to him, of Mahapajapati, of Ashoka. Not merely stories: in each one a point of Dhamma, a small piece of guidance for our daily lives.

This journey will not stop with the Buddha. Each day we will also read the story alongside the thought of our Babasaheb Ambedkar. For it was he who brought this Dhamma, which had vanished from this soil, back to our own land and to us.
I will tell each story with its source, naming the text in which it is recorded. This is not merely a time for listening; it is a time to learn, to reflect, and to grow together.
I warmly invite you all to join me on this small journey.
If there is any error in this, please tell me, and we will all learn together.

1.title: Sumedha's Vow
body: A very long time ago, in the city of Amaravati, there lived a man of great wealth named Sumedha. Realising that the wealth he had gathered would in the end be of no use, he renounced everything and went to the Himalayas as an ascetic.

In that age the Buddha Dipankara was living. One day people were repairing the road along which he was to come. Before Sumedha could finish smoothing his stretch of it, the Buddha arrived, and a patch of mud was left in that place.

Without hesitating, Sumedha spread his body and his long hair over the mud and lay down, so that the Buddha and the Sangha might walk across him. In that moment he took a great vow: I could reach liberation this very day; but I will not seek my liberation alone. However long the ages take, I too will become a Buddha and carry all beings across.
Dipankara Buddha stopped and declared: this ascetic, in an age to come, will become a Buddha by the name of Gotama. That was the beginning of the bodhisattva path, the path of living for others.
1.insight: True greatness is not seeking liberation for oneself alone; it is the compassion that waits for others.
1.ambedkar: Ambedkar chose this same way. Though he could have lived alone with fame and office, he gave his whole life to the liberation of his people. Like Sumedha's vow, Ambedkar's life was a vow taken for a collective liberation.
1.source: Buddhavamsa (Khuddaka Nikaya); the introduction to the Jataka book, the Nidanakatha.

2.title: The Birth of Siddhartha
body: In north India, on what is now the border of Nepal, there was a small republic ruled by the Sakya clan. It worked as a gana-sangha, a council: not a monarchy where one man rules, but a body where many gather to decide. The head of that council was Suddhodana; his wife was Mayadevi.
Around the sixth century BCE, a son was born to them at Lumbini. They named the child Siddhartha, meaning 'one who accomplishes his purpose'. The clan name was Gautama.
Within a few days of the birth, his mother Mayadevi died. After that it was her sister, Mahapajapati Gotami, who raised Siddhartha with love.

His father Suddhodana wanted his son to become a leader, a ruler. So he raised him amid comforts, shielded from the bitterness of life. But it was neither this comfortable birth nor this upbringing that made Siddhartha a great man; it was the understanding he reached later, when he saw the world outside, searched for the cause of suffering, and thought it through for himself, that made him the Buddha.
2.insight: A person's greatness does not lie in where or how they were born; it lies in the truth they discover and the work they do. The Buddha was born not as an avatar but as a human being like us, and that is what gives us confidence.
2.ambedkar: In his book The Buddha and His Dhamma, Ambedkar presented the Buddha as a human being: one who thought, struggled and found the truth for himself. This humanist idea, that birth does not determine a person's worth, became the foundation stone of his struggle against caste hierarchy. And in that Sakya council system Ambedkar saw the roots of Indian democracy.
2.source: Ambedkar, The Buddha and His Dhamma (the section on Siddhartha's human birth); passages in the Tipitaka where the Buddha declares himself a human being.

3.title: The Great Renunciation
body: Siddhartha grew up as a prince amid pleasures. But those comforts did not quench the thirst of his mind. Seeing the truths of old age, sickness and death, he began to think deeply about what caused them.

Ambedkar also put forward a concrete social cause for this. War was about to break out between the Sakyas and the Koliyas over the waters of the river Rohini. The young Siddhartha opposed that war; but the Sakya assembly chose war. Refusing to accept violence, he faced a hard choice: submit to the assembly's decision, or leave the country. In the end, it was in opposition to violence that he left home.
At twenty-nine he left the palace, leaving his wife Yasodhara and his son Rahula, and set out on the path of seeking.
3.insight: Comforts do not quench the thirst of the mind; real peace is born in inward searching and in taking a stand against injustice.
3.ambedkar: By Ambedkar's reading, the Buddha's renunciation was not mere personal weariness; it was a social and ethical refusal, a stand against violence and injustice. Dhamma does not withdraw from the problems of society but faces them directly. That is Ambedkar's Navayana view.
3.source: Ariyapariyesana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 26); Ambedkar, The Buddha and His Dhamma (the section on the Rohini river conflict and the great renunciation).

4.title: Austerity and Sujata's Gift
body: Having left home, Siddhartha learned deep meditation from the sages of the time, Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta. But realising it did not give final liberation, he left them. He then practised severe austerities in the forest with five companions. He cut his food away almost entirely and wore his body down to a skeleton. Six years passed like this, and understanding did not come.

One day, weak and fainting, a truth became clear to him: to torment the body is itself an extreme; like indulgence, this too is one end. It is the middle way, the moderate path, that leads to awakening.

At that moment a village woman named Sujata brought and offered him milk rice. Siddhartha accepted and ate it. Seeing him abandon severe austerity, the five companions left him. But Siddhartha recovered his strength and, with a clear mind, moved towards understanding.
4.insight: Both extremes, excess of pleasure and excess of torment, lead astray. Understanding lies in the middle way.
4.ambedkar: The Buddha rejected superstition and self-mortification and chose reason and moderation. Ambedkar too rejected caste, superstition and useless custom, and gave people a Dhamma founded on knowledge and reason.

5.title: Awakening Under the Bodhi Tree
body: At a place called Uruvela, under a pipal tree, Siddhartha sat down. He resolved that he would not rise from that place until he had seen the truth.

Then inward forces, fear, desire, doubt and pride, shook his mind. Tradition calls these Mara. Siddhartha did not move; he touched the earth and called it as witness to his path. Those inner disturbances subsided.
That night his mind grew clear, and he saw the deep truths of life: suffering, its cause, its ending, and the way to that ending. At dawn he rose as the Buddha, the one who has awakened.
5.insight: The enemy to be conquered is not outside; it is our own desire, fear and pride that must be overcome.
5.ambedkar: Ambedkar saw Mara not as a demon but as a symbol of the inward weaknesses of human beings and of the injustices of society. Awakening is knowing these and overcoming them.
5.source: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36); Padhana Sutta (Sutta Nipata).

6.title: The First Discourse at Sarnath
body: Having reached understanding, the Buddha went to the deer park at Sarnath in search of the five companions who had left him. At first they meant to ignore him, but seeing his calm bearing they sat down and listened.

The Buddha turned his first discourse, the wheel of Dhamma. He spoke the four noble truths: there is suffering; suffering has a cause; that cause can be removed; and there is a way to do it, the eightfold path.

Hearing that middle way which avoids both excess of pleasure and excess of torment, Kondanna was the first to see the truth. It was here that the Sangha was born, the community of those who walk the path of Dhamma.
6.insight: Dhamma is to accept suffering without denying it, to know its cause, and to walk the way that removes it.
6.ambedkar: Ambedkar widened 'suffering' beyond individual distress of mind to include the suffering produced by poverty, oppression and social injustice. He did not accept the pessimism of 'life is suffering'; suffering is real, but if its cause is changed it can also be removed. That confidence is the social outlook of Navayana.

7.title: Yasa and the First Lay Disciples
body: In Varanasi there lived a wealthy young man named Yasa. Though surrounded by pleasures, one night at midnight they seemed empty to him. Crying out 'What distress! What sorrow!' he left the house.
The Buddha saw him and said, 'Here there is no distress; come here, sit.' Those quietly spoken words changed Yasa. Hearing the Dhamma, he came to clarity.

His father, who had come searching for Yasa, also heard the Dhamma and took refuge in the Buddha: the first lay disciple. Yasa's mother and wife became the first women lay disciples. More than fifty of Yasa's friends took ordination.
It became clear here that Dhamma is not for monastics alone but for householders too, for women and men, for everyone.
7.insight: Dhamma does not belong to one group alone; it can be lived and understood in any station of life.
7.ambedkar: Ambedkar did not accept a Dhamma shut away in palaces and monasteries. It is for ordinary people, he said: a living way that gives dignity and freedom to the farmer, the worker, the woman, to everyone.

8.title: Sariputta and Moggallana
body: Upatissa (Sariputta) and Kolita (Moggallana) were two friends who had gone to many teachers in search of truth and found no satisfaction. They had promised each other that whoever found the truth first would tell the other.

One day Sariputta was struck by the calm walk of Assaji, a disciple of the Buddha. He asked, 'What does your teacher teach?' Assaji answered simply: all things arise from a cause; the Buddha shows that cause, and how those things come to an end.

In those few words the truth became clear to Sariputta. He ran and told his friend. Both joined the Buddha. Sariputta later became the disciple foremost in wisdom, and Moggallana the one foremost in concentration.
8.insight: A genuine search is not rigid; even in simple words a deep truth can shine out.
8.ambedkar: Ambedkar valued the Buddha's principle of cause and effect greatly, because it rejected fate and divine agency and made human action and circumstance the cause. The confidence that if conditions are changed the outcomes can also be changed is the foundation of social transformation.

9.title: Mahakassapa, Guardian of the Dhamma
body: Mahakassapa was born into a family of great wealth. But drawn neither to wealth nor to household life, he wanted the simple life of renunciation. As soon as he met the Buddha he knew this was his teacher, and became a disciple.
He was foremost in strict discipline and in simplicity; leaving costly cloth aside, he wore a robe made of rags. The Buddha himself once honoured him by inviting him to sit on his own seat.

After the Buddha's passing, Mahakassapa took on the duty of keeping the Dhamma from scattering. He himself presided over the first council, and the Buddha's teachings were preserved for the generations.
9.insight: Simplicity and discipline are not mere restraint; they are the strength that protects the Dhamma.
9.ambedkar: Mahakassapa protected a Dhamma that was in decline and carried it across to later generations. In the same way Ambedkar, in the twentieth century, recovered and gave new life to a Buddhism that had all but disappeared in India: the guardian of the Dhamma for the modern age.
9.source: Theragatha; Samyutta Nikaya; Anguttara Nikaya (Etadagga section).

10.title: Ananda, the Humble Attendant
body: Ananda was the Buddha's cousin. For more than twenty years he was the Buddha's personal attendant, hearing every discourse he gave and fixing it in his mind. His memory was extraordinary.

When he accepted the role of attendant, Ananda set some conditions: he wanted no special food or robe for himself; but the discourses the Buddha gave, including those spoken when he was not present, must be repeated to him. His service was without self-interest.
At the first council after the Buddha's passing, it was Ananda who recited the discourses, beginning 'Thus have I heard'. It is because of his memory that we have the suttas today.
10.insight: Humble, selfless service, even when it is quiet, protects what belongs to the generations.
10.ambedkar: It was Ananda who opened the way for women to take their place in the Sangha. His manner of speaking up on behalf of those who were kept out recalls Ambedkar, who spent his life speaking for the rights of women (the Hindu Code Bill) and for the rights of the oppressed.

11.title: Mahapajapati Gotami and the Bhikkhuni Sangha
body: Mahapajapati Gotami was the sister of the Buddha's mother, and the foster mother who raised Siddhartha after Mayadevi's death. After the Buddha's awakening, she too wished to enter the path of Dhamma. She asked permission for women to renounce and join the Sangha.

The Buddha hesitated at first. Mahapajapati did not give up. She shaved her head, put on ochre robes, and walked with many women all the way to Vesali, standing at the gate with swollen feet and tears in her eyes.

Ananda asked on her behalf: 'Are women also able to reach understanding on the path of Dhamma?' The Buddha said, 'They are able.' Then let the way be opened for them too, said Ananda. The Buddha agreed; Mahapajapati became the first bhikkhuni, and the order of women was born. In an age when liberation through knowledge was denied to women, this was a revolution.
11.insight: Liberation and understanding are not bounded by gender; when the mind is ready, the way opens.
11.ambedkar: Ambedkar stressed strongly that the Buddha had accepted women as having equal right to liberation through understanding. He himself framed the Hindu Code Bill for the rights of women, and resigned his ministry when it was blocked. Equality, in gender as in caste, is the heart of his Dhamma.
11.source: Vinaya Cullavagga X; Anguttara Nikaya 8.51; Therigatha.

12.title: Khema, Foremost in Wisdom
body: Khema was the queen of King Bimbisara of Magadha, famed for her extraordinary beauty. Proud of that beauty, she hesitated to meet the Buddha, thinking he would speak slightingly of it. One day the king gently brought her to him.

The Buddha made a simple truth plain to her: youth and beauty ripen with time, weaken, and vanish. Nothing is permanent. Khema saw clearly that beauty is impermanent. Her attachment to her own form dissolved, and her mind grew clear.
She later took ordination and became foremost in wisdom among the bhikkhunis; even kings came to her with deep questions.
12.insight: When attachment to outward appearance falls away, inward wisdom begins to shine.
12.ambedkar: In the Buddha's Dhamma a woman, even a queen, reached the summit of wisdom. Not birth, beauty or office, but understanding determines worth. This is the root of Ambedkar's call to 'educate': that knowledge is liberation.

13.title: Uppalavanna
body: Uppalavanna was the daughter of a wealthy man; she was given that name for her complexion, like a blue lotus. Many sorrows and betrayals befell her in life, and she was wronged by those closest to her. Wearied by the cruelties of life, she took ordination.
In deep meditation her mind grew clear; the sorrows of the past did not hold her. She became foremost among the bhikkhunis in firmness and clarity of mind.

Once, while she was meditating alone in the forest, a man tried to harm her. But her firmness and clarity of mind did not break. Her life showed that whatever the past has been, an awakened mind cannot be brought low.
13.insight: The sorrows of the past need not define us; an awakened mind rises above them.
13.ambedkar: Uppalavanna's life shows that those whom society has pushed down and made to suffer can also reach the summit through understanding and discipline. This echoes Ambedkar's conviction that a degraded condition is not permanent; it can be changed.

14.title: Patacara, Awakening Through Grief
body: Patacara was the daughter of a wealthy man. Life dealt with her cruelly and without pause: she lost one child in childbirth, another in a flood, and her husband to a snakebite. Returning to her town, she heard that her parents and brother had died when their house collapsed. Unable to bear the grief, she lost her senses and wandered the streets without clothing.
One day she reached the place where the Buddha was teaching the Dhamma. He did not drive her away; he said, 'Sister, regain your clarity.' That kind voice brought her back.

The Buddha made a truth plain to her: the tears human beings have shed in life are more than the water of all the oceans. Grief is not yours alone. In that clarity Patacara found peace; she took ordination and came to understanding.
14.insight: Do not carry grief in isolation; when its truth is known and accepted, it becomes liberation.
14.ambedkar: Ambedkar too passed through great loss and grief in his own life. But he turned his grief into work for his people. Dhamma is not only a refuge in suffering but also a way of transforming it into something constructive.

15.title: Kisagotami and the Mustard Seed
body: Kisagotami's only son died while still a small child. Her mind unhinged by grief, she carried the dead child about and wandered the town asking for medicine that would bring her son back to life. Someone sent her to the Buddha.

The Buddha said quietly: 'Bring me a handful of mustard seed, but from a house where no one has ever died.' Kisagotami went from house to house full of hope. Mustard seed there was in every house; but there was not one house that death had not touched. In every house, a story of grief.

Little by little the truth became clear to her: death is common to all, and she did not suffer alone. In that clarity she buried her child, took refuge in the Buddha, and walked towards understanding.
15.insight: Suffering is not solitary; it is something the whole of humanity shares. That recognition is both consolation and solidarity.
15.ambedkar: The recognition that suffering is shared is what gives rise to collective feeling and unity. This is the depth of Ambedkar's call to 'organise': that oppression can be resisted not separately but only together.

16.title: Visakha, the Great Giver
body: Visakha was a woman of a wealthy family who met the Buddha as a child and understood the Dhamma. After her marriage took her to Savatthi, she became the greatest supporter of the Buddhist Sangha. Selling her priceless ornament, she built a large vihara for the monastics, known as the Eastern Monastery.
She asked the Buddha for, and received, permission to provide many things during the rains: robes, medicine, food for the monastics, and care for the sick.
It was not giving alone; Visakha also asked searching questions and understood the Dhamma deeply. Living as a householder, and as a woman, she stood as a pillar of the Sangha.
16.insight: Giving is not merely material; it is largeness of heart and social responsibility.
16.ambedkar: Visakha, a laywoman, led from the front in social work and leadership. Dhamma should not be shut inside monasteries but should serve society, and women should take the lead: this is exactly the engaged, socially minded Dhamma Ambedkar wanted.

17.title: Anathapindika and the Jetavana
body: Anathapindika was a man of great wealth in the city of Savatthi. His name means 'one who feeds the destitute', given because he helped the poor and those without support continuously. Once he met the Buddha, his life changed.

He wanted an excellent place in Savatthi for the Buddha and the Sangha to stay. Prince Jeta's park was the only suitable ground. The prince said in jest, 'Cover the whole park with gold coins and I will give it to you.' Anathapindika actually began bringing cartloads of gold and laying them out.
Astonished at his resolve, the prince gave him the park and himself donated a portion. There the famous vihara called Jetavana arose, the place where the Buddha spent many rainy seasons.
17.insight: The true value of wealth is not in hoarding it but in sharing it well.
17.ambedkar: Anathapindika's very name tells of his service to the poor and the unsupported. This is a fine illustration of Ambedkar's view that Dhamma is interwoven with social welfare: compassion is not a feeling but an act.

18.title: Angulimala, from Killer to Arahant
body: Ahimsaka was a gifted student; but led astray by a plot against him, he became a terrible killer. He was called Angulimala because he wore the fingers of those he had killed as a garland. People trembled at his name.
One day the Buddha walked calmly along his forest road. Angulimala chased him with a sword; but however hard he ran, he could not catch up with the walking Buddha. Bewildered, he shouted, 'Stop!'

The Buddha said quietly: 'I stopped long ago, Angulimala. I have stopped at violence. It is you who have not stopped.' Those words split him open. He threw down his sword, fell at the Buddha's feet and took ordination. Even when people stoned him for the cruelties of his past, he bore it patiently, held to his discipline, and became an arahant, one who has awakened.
18.insight: No one is beyond change. However dark the past, the way to transformation always stays open.
18.ambedkar: The Buddha accepted and raised up those whom society had cast out and branded as evil. Neither birth nor past decides a person's worth permanently. This is strong ground for Ambedkar's principle that human dignity is inalienable.

19.title: King Bimbisara and Ajatasattu
body: King Bimbisara of Magadha was an early supporter of the Buddha. Drawn to Siddhartha when he saw him wandering as an ascetic, he asked him to come to him once he had reached understanding. He later gave the Buddha the park called Veluvana.

But his son Ajatasattu, greedy for power and incited by Devadatta, imprisoned his father and caused his death. Even with power in his hands, his mind found no peace; the wrong he had done tormented him.

In the end Ajatasattu went to the Buddha. The Buddha did not despise him; he explained the Dhamma and showed him that acknowledging one's own wrong is the beginning of change. His story teaches that ethics endures where power does not.
19.insight: Power and success without ethics bring no peace; acknowledging the wrong one has done is the first step of change.
19.ambedkar: This story teaches that rule and power must rest on justice. When Ambedkar framed the Indian Constitution, he made it the foundation that power should not be arbitrary but bounded by justice and equality.

20.title: Jivaka, the Buddha's Physician
body: Jivaka was found and raised as an abandoned child. He went to Takshashila to study medicine and became the finest physician of his age. He treated kings and ordinary people with the same compassion.

Jivaka served as personal physician to the Buddha and the Sangha by his own choice. He donated his own mango grove to the Sangha. Once he gave his finest perfumed cloth to the Buddha, and so opened the way for householders to offer robes.

He showed by his life that medicine is not merely a trade but a service. The Buddha himself said that to care for a sick monastic is the same as caring for the Buddha; Jivaka's service was that principle made visible.
20.insight: Service does not look at caste, office or wealth; helping those who suffer is the highest Dhamma.
20.ambedkar: Jivaka treated the king and the poor with the same compassion, with no difference in regard. Ambedkar, who lived for the welfare of the oppressed, held the same conviction: no human being is unworthy of service and of dignity.
20.source: Vinaya Mahavagga (the medical section); Jivaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 55).

21.title: Ambapali's Gift
body: Ambapali was the celebrated courtesan of the city of Vesali. Society saw her through a particular lens; but she excelled in wealth and in art. When the Buddha came to Vesali, Ambapali met him and invited him to take his meal at her house the next day. The Buddha accepted.
On his way back, the wealthy princes of the city asked for the same favour. Though they offered a great sum, Ambapali refused: 'Even if you gave me the whole city I would not give up this favour.'
Everyone was astonished that the Buddha had accepted a courtesan's invitation ahead of the princes'. Ambapali later gave her mango grove to the Sangha, took ordination, and reached understanding.
21.insight: A person's worth is not in their occupation or social position, but in purity of heart and in what they do.
21.ambedkar: The Buddha accepted the invitation of a woman society held in contempt ahead of that of wealthy princes. This principle, that human dignity does not depend on social status, is at the centre of Ambedkar's struggle against caste degradation.
21.source: Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 16); Vinaya Mahavagga; Therigatha.

22.title: Rahula, the Buddha's Son
body: Rahula was Siddhartha's son; he was an infant when his father renounced. When the Buddha returned after his awakening, his mother Yasodhara sent Rahula to him saying, 'Ask for your inheritance.' The Buddha gave him not wealth but the Dhamma, and admitted him to the order.

As a boy, Rahula sometimes told small lies in play. One day the Buddha showed him the water left after washing his feet and said, 'The renunciant life of one who lies is as empty as this dirty water.' That simple lesson fixed the value of truth deep in Rahula's mind.
Learning and practising steadily, and holding to his discipline, Rahula became the disciple foremost in training.
22.insight: Truth is the foundation of conduct; education and practice are what refine a person.
22.ambedkar: The Buddha made education and Dhamma, not wealth, his son's inheritance. In Ambedkar's call, 'Educate, Agitate, Organise', education comes first; it is the greatest asset in a people's liberation.

23.title: Nanda, the Buddha's Brother
body: Nanda was the Buddha's cousin. On the day his marriage was to take place, the Buddha put his alms bowl in Nanda's hand and led him to the vihara. Nanda took ordination while still longing for his bride, and his mind found no peace.
Knowing Nanda's longing, the Buddha used a comparison to show him how impermanent his desire was. Step by step he made clear that attachment to physical beauty becomes empty with time.
Once the truth was clear, Nanda held to the path of Dhamma not through outward pressure but through inward conviction. Overcoming desire and mastering his mind, he came to understanding.
23.insight: Attachment to outward beauty is impermanent; knowing and mastering the mind is real strength.
23.ambedkar: Dhamma must take root through inward conviction, not outward compulsion. Ambedkar did not impose Buddhism on people; he put it forward as a way to be chosen with understanding and with self-respect.

24.title: Devadatta, a Cautionary Tale
body: Devadatta was a relative of the Buddha and a monk who had joined the Sangha. But over time greed and envy took root in him. He wanted the leadership of the Sangha for himself.
When the Buddha refused, Devadatta conspired with King Ajatasattu; he even tried to have the Buddha killed. He also tried to split the Sangha. But each of his schemes ended in failure.
In the end, isolated and in failing health, he came to see the wrongs he had done and regretted them. Devadatta stands as a warning of where greed for power and envy will take a person.
24.insight: Greed, envy and pride are poisons that destroy oneself; power does not stand above Dhamma.
24.ambedkar: This story warns against those who use religion and power for their own interest. Ambedkar criticised sharply the making of religion into an instrument for dividing and exploiting people; Dhamma is for liberation, not for domination.

25.title: The Taming of Nalagiri
body: As part of his plotting, Devadatta had the maddened wild elephant Nalagiri given liquor and set loose on the street the Buddha was walking along, in order to kill him. The elephant came trumpeting towards the Buddha, smashing everything in its way. People screamed and ran; the disciples told the Buddha to step back.
But the Buddha stood without moving. Without fear or hatred, he directed boundless compassion, metta, towards that elephant.

Nalagiri, which had come in fury, weakened before the Buddha's calm compassion. Its charge slowed, it came near, lowered its head and bowed at his feet. This is the sight of violence conquered not by violence but by compassion.
25.insight: Fury is not overcome by counter-fury; calm compassion is the greatest strength.
25.ambedkar: Ambedkar chose not violence but a calm and steady way: constitution, law, education, democratic struggle. His conviction was that this ethical path, holding both compassion and reason, is what brings lasting change.

26.title: The Mahaparinibbana
body: Having reached eighty years, the Buddha undertook his final journey. He walked on, teaching the Dhamma all along the way. Near Kusinara, after a meal taken at a smith's house, his body weakened; he knew his end was near.
To the grieving Ananda the Buddha said in consolation: 'All that has arisen will pass away; this is nature. Do not think of it as losing me. The Dhamma I have taught is your teacher.'

Then he gave that imperishable last teaching: 'Be a lamp unto yourselves (atta-dipa); take the Dhamma as your lamp. Seek no other refuge. All things are impermanent; strive on with awareness.' Having spoken thus, between two sal trees, he passed peacefully into nibbana.
26.insight: Be a light unto yourself; depend on no one else, but trust your own understanding and your own effort.
26.ambedkar: This teaching of self-reliance, 'be a light unto yourself', is the heart of Ambedkar's way. Trust not a god or fate, but your own effort and your own understanding. His call, 'Educate, Agitate, Organise', is that same self-reliance in another form.

27.title: The First Council
body: After the Buddha's passing there was fear that the teachings he had given might scatter. Some even said, 'Now we may live without restraint.' Seeing this, Mahakassapa convened a great assembly at Rajagaha, the first council, to gather and preserve the Dhamma.

Five hundred arahants assembled. Upali recited the rules of discipline the Buddha had laid down (the Vinaya). Ananda recited the discourses he had heard (the Suttas), one by one, beginning 'Thus have I heard'. Those assembled agreed them and set them down.
It is because of this collective effort that the words the Buddha spoke have reached us across twenty-five centuries.
27.insight: More than individual effort, it is organised collective effort that makes knowledge endure.
27.ambedkar: That collective effort, which gathered, defined and preserved the Dhamma for later generations, shows the strength of organisation. Ambedkar too gathered and set down the justice of a nation as a constitution; his call to 'organise' comes from the same sense of organisation.

28.title: Ashoka, from the Sword to the Dhamma
body: Ashoka was the powerful ruler of the Mauryan empire. In his desire to extend it, he launched a devastating war against the country of Kalinga. Hundreds of thousands were killed; many more perished wounded or driven from their homes.

Seeing the heaps of the dead spread across the field of victory, and hearing the crying, Ashoka's heart broke. Victory brought him not joy but deep anguish. He understood that what is won by the sword is not true victory.
From that moment, 'Chandashoka', Ashoka the cruel, became 'Dhammashoka', Ashoka of the Dhamma; he laid down the sword and took up the Dhamma.
28.insight: True victory is not the defeat of others; it is renouncing violence and taking up compassion.
28.ambedkar: Ashoka made the Dhamma the ethic of the state and built a rule of compassion. The wheel of Dhamma on his pillar, the emblem of ethical conduct, stands today at the centre of the Indian flag. Ambedkar was a member of the committee (chaired by Rajendra Prasad) that chose that national flag.

29.title: Ashoka's Dhamma: Edicts and Pillars
body: Having changed his mind, Ashoka did not leave the Dhamma in words but made it the work of government. He had his principles carved into rocks and stone pillars and set up across the empire, so that people could read and know them.

The counsel he gave in those inscriptions: compassion towards all beings; respect for parents and elders; good conduct towards servants; respect for all religions. He extended public works widely: hospitals for people and for animals, trees along the roads, wells, rest houses.
Ashoka showed that a ruler should take pride not in conquests but in the welfare of his people. The lion pillar he raised at Sarnath is today the national emblem of India.
29.insight: Dhamma is not mere belief; it is compassion, respect and public good, an ethic lived out in life.
29.ambedkar: Ashoka shaped the Dhamma as a social ethic of compassion, equality, tolerance and public welfare. This anticipates Ambedkar's view that Dhamma is not celestial philosophy but justice in this world. Ashoka's lion pillar and wheel of Dhamma are today the emblems of our nation.
29.source: The rock and pillar edicts of Ashoka.

30.title: Mahinda and Sanghamitta
body: Ashoka did not stop the Dhamma at his own country; he sent emissaries across the world. The closest among them were his own son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitta, both of whom had taken ordination.
Mahinda went to Sri Lanka and led King Devanampiya Tissa and his people onto the path of Dhamma. Later, when the women of Sri Lanka also wished to take ordination, it was Sanghamitta who had to go.

When Sanghamitta went to Sri Lanka she carried with her a sapling of the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya under which the Buddha had reached understanding. Planted at Anuradhapura, that sapling still grows today, one of the oldest trees in the world whose year of planting is known: witness that the Dhamma took root across the sea.
30.insight: True understanding is not shut inside oneself; it is shared, so that it takes root in the lives of others too.
30.ambedkar: Mahinda and Sanghamitta carried the Dhamma from India to Sri Lanka. Centuries later, Ambedkar brought that same Dhamma, which had declined in India itself, back to the soil of its birth; the journey completed a full circle.

31.title: Ambedkar: the Dhamma Returns to India
body: The path the Buddha showed shone in India for many centuries; but in time it declined in the very land of its birth. About two thousand five hundred years later, one man brought that Dhamma back to life.

Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar (1891-1956) was born into the Mahar community, held to be 'untouchable'. From childhood he met with the humiliations of caste; he was made to sit apart at school and was refused even the touch of water. But he turned those humiliations into a fire of learning. He took doctorates at Columbia and at the University of London and became one of the most learned Indians of his time, and the principal architect of the constitution of independent India.

Seeking a path of equality and reason by which to be free of caste oppression with dignity, he found it in the Buddha's Dhamma. At Yeola in 1935 he declared, 'I was born a Hindu, that was not in my hands; but I will not die a Hindu.' After years of deep study he wrote his great work, The Buddha and His Dhamma.

On 14 October 1956, at Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur, in a ceremony conducted by the senior Burmese monk Mahasthavir Chandramani, Ambedkar took refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha together with about three hundred and sixty-five thousand people. He gave his people twenty-two vows, founded on equality, reason and compassion. About two months later, on 6 December 1956, he died; but the lamp he lit has not gone out.

A Tamil Nadu connection: even before Ambedkar, in 1898, Pandit Iyothee Thass founded the Sakya Buddhist Society in Tamil Nadu and began the Buddhist revival here: the Tamil land's own Buddhist history.
31.insight: Dhamma is not bounded by birth or caste. 'By birth no one is low and no one is high; it is by action alone,' said the Buddha, and Ambedkar lived it out.
31.ambedkar: This thirty-one day journey begins with Sumedha's vow and ends with Ambedkar: a full circle in which the Dhamma returns to the soil of its birth. For Ambedkar, Dhamma is a living path of dignity, equality and liberation.
31.source: The Buddha and His Dhamma (Ambedkar, 1957); Annihilation of Caste (1936); Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches.
